cards.title: Needs come first
cards.text: Needs are the things you must pay for: rent, food, bills and travel to uni.

cards.title: Wants can wait
cards.text: Wants are nice to have, like takeaways, gigs and new clothes. Pay for them from what is left after your needs.

cards.title: Cut the cost of needs
cards.text: Needs still have cheaper versions. Shared rooms, own-brand food and a railcard all cut what you must spend.

facts.text: A 16-25 Railcard costs £35 for a year and takes a third off most rail fares.
facts.source_label: 16-25 Railcard

facts.text: A home where everyone is a full-time student gets a 100% council tax discount, so pays nothing.
facts.source_label: gov.uk · Council Tax discounts for students

quiz.text: Which of these is a need?
Your money runs short this month. What do you cut first?
Travel to uni is a need. How can you make it cheaper?

answers.explanation: Rent keeps a roof over your head. The others are nice to have.
Takeaways are a want. Food and rent are needs.
A 16-25 Railcard takes a third off most rail fares.

cards.title: Know what comes in
cards.text: Add up all the money you get: loan, bursary, part-time pay and help from family.

cards.title: Know what goes out
cards.text: List rent, bills, food and travel first. What is left is for everything else.

cards.title: Small amounts add up
cards.text: A small cost you pay every month adds up over a year. Cutting one regular cost often beats one big saving.

facts.text: In England your maintenance loan comes in 3 payments a year, one at the start of each term.
facts.source_label: gov.uk · Student finance: how you're assessed and paid

facts.text: In Scotland your living-cost loan can come monthly over 9 term-time months, or over 12 months.
facts.source_label: SAAS · Living-cost loan

facts.text: In England the most Maintenance Loan for 2026/27, living away from home outside London, is £10,830.
facts.source_label: gov.uk · Student finance for new full-time students

quiz.text: What is a budget?

choices.text: A plan for money in and money out

quiz.text: Your loan arrives once a term. What should you do?

choices.text: Spend it in the first week
Split it across the weeks until the next payment

quiz.text: Which saves more over a year: £20 a month or £200 once?

answers.explanation: A budget shows what comes in and what you plan to spend.
The loan must last the whole term, so split it by the weeks it covers.
£20 a month is £240 a year, which is more than £200.

cards.title: Small costs repeat
cards.text: A £10 monthly subscription costs £120 a year.

cards.title: Prices creep up
cards.text: Subscription prices often go up, so check what you pay each year.

cards.title: Cancel what you do not use
cards.text: If you have not used an app or service this month, cancel it. You can join again later.

facts.text: When you order online or by phone, you can usually cancel within 14 days. Streaming and downloads have different rules, so check before you start.
facts.source_label: gov.uk · Online and distance selling

quiz.text: You pay £8 a month for an app you never open. What does it cost in a year?
How often should you check your subscriptions?
You have not used a streaming service for two months. What do you do?

choices.text: Cancel it and join again if you need it

answers.explanation: £8 times 12 months is £96.
Prices change, so check at least once a year.
You can usually join again at any time, so you save money now.

cards.title: Every choice has a cost
cards.text: When you spend money on one thing, you cannot spend it on another.

cards.title: Money can grow
cards.text: Money you spend today cannot grow for tomorrow.

cards.title: Count the best thing you gave up
cards.text: The true cost of a choice includes the best thing you did not choose.

facts.text: Money you put in a Lifetime ISA gets a 25% bonus from the government. Spend it and you give that up.
facts.source_label: gov.uk · Lifetime ISA

quiz.text: You spend £1,000 instead of saving at 5% a year. What did you give up in year one?
What is opportunity cost?

choices.text: The best thing you gave up

quiz.text: You choose a £60 night out over a £60 train home. What is the opportunity cost?

answers.explanation: It is the value of the next best choice you did not make.
The trip home is what you gave up.

summary.title: Prices creep up
summary.locked_reason: Finish What you give up first

cards.title: Prices rise over time
cards.text: When prices rise, the same money buys less. This is called inflation.

cards.title: Pay must keep up
cards.text: If your pay rises slower than prices, you are worse off, even with a pay rise.

cards.title: Frozen limits
cards.text: When tax limits stay the same while prices and pay rise, more of your pay is taxed.

facts.text: The Bank of England's target is to keep inflation at 2% a year.
facts.source_label: Bank of England · Inflation and the 2% target

facts.text: The Personal Allowance is £12,570 a year in 2026/27. You pay no Income Tax on pay below it.
facts.source_label: gov.uk · Income Tax rates and allowances

quiz.text: Rent rises 4% and your pay rises 2%. Are you better off?
What does inflation do to cash under your bed?
Pay rises but the tax-free limit stays the same. What happens?

choices.text: More of your pay is taxed
Less of your pay is taxed

answers.explanation: Your costs grew faster than your pay, so you can afford less.
Prices go up, so the same cash buys less.
The part above the frozen limit grows, so more of your pay is taxed.

cards.title: Surprises happen
cards.text: A broken laptop or a late loan payment can come at any time.

cards.title: Cash stops debt
cards.text: Savings for surprises stop a sudden bill turning into debt.

cards.title: Start small
cards.text: Even £10 a week builds a cushion. Keep it in a separate savings account.

facts.text: Savings in a UK bank or building society are protected up to £120,000 per person if the firm fails.
facts.source_label: FSCS · Check your money is protected

facts.text: Interest on cash in an ISA is tax free. You can put in up to £20,000 a year.
facts.source_label: gov.uk · Individual Savings Accounts

quiz.text: A £500 bill arrives and you have no savings. What is the cheapest way to pay next time?
Where should your emergency money be?
What is an emergency fund for?

answers.explanation: Savings cost you no interest.
You need it fast and it must not fall in value.
It is for costs you did not plan for.

cards.title: Two loans
cards.text: The tuition loan goes straight to your uni. The maintenance loan goes to you for living costs.

cards.title: Paid in parts
cards.text: The maintenance loan comes in parts during the year, not all at once.

cards.title: Repay when you earn
cards.text: You repay a share of what you earn above a threshold, not a fixed amount. Earn less and you repay nothing.

facts.text: In England the most Maintenance Loan for 2026/27, living away from home outside London, is £10,830.
facts.source_label: gov.uk · Student finance for new full-time students

facts.text: In England the maintenance loan is paid in 3 instalments a year, one at the start of each term.
facts.source_label: gov.uk · Student finance: how you're assessed and paid

facts.text: You repay 9% of what you earn above the threshold.
facts.source_label: gov.uk · Repaying your student loan

quiz.text: Where does the tuition loan go?
You earn below the threshold. How much do you repay that month?
How often is the maintenance loan paid in England?

answers.explanation: The tuition loan is paid straight to your uni.
Below the threshold you repay nothing.
It comes in 3 instalments, one at the start of each term.

summary.title: Scholarships and bursaries
summary.locked_reason: Finish How student loans work first

cards.title: Free money
cards.text: A bursary or scholarship is money you do not pay back.

cards.title: Ask your uni
cards.text: Most bursaries come from your uni. Check its money or student support pages.

cards.title: Apply early
cards.text: Many have deadlines and some need forms. Apply as soon as you can.

facts.text: In England the most Maintenance Loan for 2026/27, living with parents, is £9,118. A bursary is extra money on top that you do not pay back.
facts.source_label: gov.uk · Student finance for new full-time students

quiz.text: Do you pay back a bursary?
Where do most bursaries come from?
When should you apply?

answers.explanation: A bursary is a gift, not a loan.
Most bursaries are run by universities.
Funds and deadlines are limited, so apply early.

cards.title: Rent is the biggest bill
cards.text: For most students, rent costs more than anything else.

cards.title: Read the contract
cards.text: Check how long you must pay rent for, and which bills are included.

cards.title: Moving costs money
cards.text: A deposit, a van and new things add up. A small rent rise can be cheaper than moving.

facts.text: A home where everyone is a full-time student gets a 100% council tax discount.
facts.source_label: gov.uk · Council Tax discounts for students

facts.text: Rent in London costs more, so the most Maintenance Loan in London is higher: £14,135 for 2026/27.
facts.source_label: gov.uk · Student finance for new full-time students

quiz.text: Your rent rises £30 a month and moving costs £900. How many months until moving pays off?
Everyone in your house is a full-time student. What council tax do you pay?
What should you check before you sign a tenancy?

answers.explanation: £900 divided by £30 is 30 months.
An all-student home gets a 100% discount.
Bills can add a lot to the real cost.

cards.title: Sharing cuts costs
cards.text: Rent and bills split between more people cost each person less.

cards.title: Agree the split
cards.text: Agree how to split bills before they arrive. Use a shared list or app.

cards.title: Life changes the budget
cards.text: Later on, a partner or a child changes what a home costs.

facts.text: If everyone in a home but one adult is a full-time student, the council tax bill is 25% lower.
facts.source_label: gov.uk · Who has to pay Council Tax

quiz.text: Which usually lowers the cost per person of a home?
When should housemates agree how to split bills?
You live with three full-time students and you work full time. What happens to the council tax bill?

answers.explanation: Rent and bills are split between more people.
Agreeing early avoids arguments and late payments.
When all but one adult are full-time students, the bill is 25% lower.

cards.title: Bills come every month
cards.text: Gas and electricity are paid monthly, even when your loan comes once a term.

cards.title: Fixed or standard
cards.text: A fixed deal keeps your unit price the same, even when the market jumps.

cards.title: Certainty costs a bit
cards.text: A fix often costs a little more than the standard price when prices are calm.

facts.text: Under the Ofgem price cap from 1 October to 31 December 2026, a typical home on gas and electricity pays £1,723 a year by Direct Debit.
facts.source_label: Ofgem · Energy price cap from 1 October 2026

facts.text: Your maintenance loan comes 3 times a year, so set aside enough from each payment for the monthly bills.
facts.source_label: gov.uk · Student finance: how you're assessed and paid

quiz.text: Energy prices are about to jump 50%. Which deal protects you?
Your loan comes once a term. How do you pay monthly bills?

choices.text: Set aside part of each payment
Pay nothing until the next loan

quiz.text: What is the downside of a fixed deal?

choices.text: It can cost a bit more when prices are calm

answers.explanation: A fixed deal keeps your price the same.
Split the loan so the bills are covered every month.
You pay a little for certainty.

cards.title: A cap on the price
cards.text: The energy price cap limits the price per unit, not your total bill.

cards.title: Use more, pay more
cards.text: If you use more energy, you still pay more.

cards.title: Cut what you use
cards.text: Shorter showers and a lower heating setting cut the bill.

facts.text: From 1 October to 31 December 2026, the cap puts a typical gas and electricity bill at £1,723 a year. Homes that use more pay more.
facts.source_label: Ofgem · Energy price cap from 1 October 2026

quiz.text: The price cap falls. Can your bill still rise?
What does the price cap limit?
Which cuts an energy bill for sure?

choices.text: Waiting for the cap to fall

answers.explanation: The cap limits the unit price, not how much you use.
It caps the unit price.
Using less is in your control.

summary.title: Shop around
summary.locked_reason: Finish The energy price cap first

cards.title: Loyalty rarely pays
cards.text: Banks and providers often give new customers better deals than old ones.

cards.title: Check once a year
cards.text: Checking your rates and deals once a year can earn you more for little effort.

cards.title: Student discounts
cards.text: Many shops, travel firms and apps give students a discount. Ask before you pay.

facts.text: A 16-25 Railcard costs £80 for 3 years, less than three 1-year cards.
facts.source_label: 16-25 Railcard

quiz.text: Your bank pays 1% and a rival pays 4% on £5,000. What is the gap in a year?
Who often gets the best deal?
How often should you check your deals?

answers.explanation: Providers often use their best deals to win new customers.
Once a year catches most price rises.

cards.title: Borrowing from your bank
cards.text: An overdraft lets you spend more than is in your account. It is a loan.

cards.title: Student overdrafts
cards.text: Many student accounts have an interest-free overdraft up to a limit. Above the limit it can cost a lot.

cards.title: It ends after uni
cards.text: The free overdraft shrinks after you graduate, so plan to pay it off.

facts.text: Since April 2020, banks can charge for an overdraft only a simple yearly interest rate, with no extra fees, so you can compare rates.
facts.source_label: FCA · Changes to overdraft charges

facts.text: Your loan comes 3 times a year. If it runs out early, an overdraft fills the gap, but you must pay it back.
facts.source_label: gov.uk · Student finance: how you're assessed and paid

quiz.text: What is an overdraft?
What happens if you go past your overdraft limit?

choices.text: It can cost a lot in fees or interest

quiz.text: What usually happens to a student overdraft after you graduate?

choices.text: It shrinks, so you must pay it back

answers.explanation: You borrow it and must pay it back.
Going over the limit is expensive.
Banks reduce the free limit over the years after uni.

cards.title: Still a debt
cards.text: Buy now, pay later splits a price into parts. You still owe all of it.

cards.title: Easy to stack up
cards.text: Several small plans at once can take a big part of your money each month.

cards.title: Late costs more
cards.text: A missed payment can bring fees and can harm your credit record.

facts.text: Since 15 July 2026 the FCA regulates Buy Now Pay Later. Lenders must check that you can afford to repay before you sign.
facts.source_label: FCA · Buy Now Pay Later

quiz.text: Is buy now, pay later a debt?
You have four plans running. What is the risk?

choices.text: They take a big part of your money each month

quiz.text: What can happen if you miss a payment?

choices.text: Fees and harm to your credit record

answers.explanation: You owe the rest of the price.
Small payments add up when you stack plans.
Late payments can cost money and count against you.

summary.title: Credit cards
summary.locked_reason: Finish Buy now, pay later first

cards.title: Clear it in full
cards.text: If you pay the full balance each month, a credit card charges no interest.

cards.title: The minimum trap
cards.text: Paying only the minimum can take years and cost more than you borrowed.

cards.title: Build a record
cards.text: Using a card a little and paying it off in full builds a good credit record.

facts.text: The Bank of England's Bank Rate is 3.75%. Credit card interest rates are usually many times higher.
facts.source_label: Bank of England · Interest rates and Bank Rate

quiz.text: You pay only the minimum each month. What happens to the interest you pay?
How do you avoid credit card interest?

choices.text: Pay the full balance each month

quiz.text: Which builds a good credit record?

choices.text: Small spending paid off in full

answers.explanation: Interest is charged on what you still owe.
No balance left means no interest.
Paying on time shows lenders you are reliable.

cards.title: Borrowing costs money
cards.text: Most debt charges interest every month you owe it.

cards.title: Pay the dearest first
cards.text: Paying off the debt with the highest interest rate first saves the most.

cards.title: Student loans are different
cards.text: A student loan is repaid from your pay, and only when you earn above a threshold.

facts.text: On a student loan you repay 9% of what you earn above a threshold, and nothing when you earn less.
facts.source_label: gov.uk · Repaying your student loan

facts.text: A Plan 2 student loan charges interest of up to 6% a year, so the balance can grow while you study.
facts.source_label: gov.uk · Repaying your student loan

quiz.text: You have a card at 20% and savings at 4%. What should you pay off first?
Which debt should you pay off first?

choices.text: The one with the highest interest

quiz.text: How is a student loan repaid?

choices.text: A share of pay above a threshold

answers.explanation: The card costs far more than the savings earn.
The highest rate costs you the most each month.
You repay 9% of what you earn above the threshold.

summary.title: Spot a scam
summary.locked_reason: Finish Good and bad debt first

cards.title: Too good to be true
cards.text: Returns far above normal rates are a warning sign.

cards.title: Your bank will not ask
cards.text: Your bank will never ask you to move money to a safe account or give your PIN.

cards.title: Stop and check
cards.text: Hang up, then call your bank on the number on your card.

facts.text: The FSCS protects up to £120,000 per person if a UK bank fails. Money you move to a fake safe account is not in your bank any more.
facts.source_label: FSCS · Check your money is protected

quiz.text: A caller says your account is at risk and asks you to move money. What do you do?

choices.text: Hang up and call the bank

quiz.text: Someone offers 20% a month with no risk. What is it?
A text asks you to log in through a link. What is safest?

answers.explanation: Banks never ask you to move money to a safe account.
No safe investment pays that.
Links in texts can lead to fake sites.

cards.title: Small cost, big cover
cards.text: Insurance turns a rare big loss into a small regular cost.

cards.title: The excess
cards.text: The excess is the part you still pay when you claim.

cards.title: Check what you have
cards.text: Your phone or your belongings may already be covered by a family or bank policy.

facts.text: If an insurer fails, the FSCS repays 90% of a valid home, travel or pet insurance claim, and compulsory cover in full.
facts.source_label: FSCS · Insurance protection

quiz.text: What is the excess on a policy?
What does insurance do?

choices.text: Turns a big loss into a small regular cost

quiz.text: Before you buy phone cover, what should you check?

answers.explanation: You pay the excess when you claim.
You pay a little often to avoid a big loss.
You may already have cover through family or your bank.

cards.title: Big swings
cards.text: Crypto prices can rise or fall by more than half in one year.

cards.title: Only what you can lose
cards.text: Only put in money you can afford to lose.

cards.title: No safety net
cards.text: Crypto is not covered like money in a UK bank.

facts.text: Money in a UK bank is protected up to £120,000 per person if the bank fails. Crypto has no such cover.
facts.source_label: FSCS · Check your money is protected

quiz.text: How much should you put in something that can halve in a year?
Can crypto lose half its value in a year?
Should you borrow to buy crypto?

answers.explanation: Only risk money you can afford to lose.
It has done so many times.
You could lose the money and still owe the debt.

cards.title: Being ill can cost pay
cards.text: Time off sick can cut your pay if your employer pays only statutory sick pay.

cards.title: Cheap habits help
cards.text: Walking, cooking and sleep protect both your health and your money.

cards.title: Know your rights
cards.text: Check your contract for sick pay before you need it.

facts.text: Statutory Sick Pay is up to £123.25 a week, for up to 28 weeks.
facts.source_label: gov.uk · Statutory Sick Pay

quiz.text: Statutory sick pay is usually...
Where do you find your sick pay rules?
Which habit protects both health and money?

answers.explanation: Statutory sick pay is lower than most wages.
Your contract says what your employer pays.
Walking is free and good for you.

cards.title: Cover for your pay
cards.text: Income protection insurance pays part of your salary if illness stops you working.

cards.title: Savings come first
cards.text: Savings of a few months do the same job for short gaps.

facts.text: If your employer pays only Statutory Sick Pay, you get up to £123.25 a week. Income protection can top this up.
facts.source_label: gov.uk · Statutory Sick Pay

quiz.text: What does income protection replace?
What covers a short gap in pay best?
When does income protection pay out?

answers.explanation: It pays part of your salary while you cannot work.
Savings cost no interest.
It is for illness or injury.

cards.title: Interest earns interest
cards.text: Interest added to savings earns interest the next year too.

cards.title: Time does the work
cards.text: The earlier you start, the more years your money has to grow.

cards.title: Debt grows the same way
cards.text: Debt compounds too, so it grows if you do not pay it.

facts.text: You can save up to £20,000 a year in ISAs, and the interest is tax free.
facts.source_label: gov.uk · Individual Savings Accounts

facts.text: A Lifetime ISA bonus can add up to £1,000 a year, and that bonus grows too.
facts.source_label: gov.uk · Lifetime ISA

quiz.text: £1,000 earns 5% a year. After two years, is it more or less than £1,100?
Who gains most from compound interest?
What happens to unpaid debt over time?

answers.explanation: Year two earns interest on £1,050, so you get £1,102.50.
More years means more growth.
Interest is added to what you owe.

cards.title: Beat rising prices
cards.text: If your savings earn less than inflation, they buy less each year.

cards.title: The real return
cards.text: The real return is the interest rate minus the inflation rate.

facts.text: The Bank of England aims to keep inflation at 2% a year. Savings must earn more than that to grow in real terms.
facts.source_label: Bank of England · Inflation and the 2% target

facts.text: If you earn little, up to £5,000 of savings interest a year can be tax free.
facts.source_label: gov.uk · Income Tax rates and allowances

quiz.text: Savings earn 2% and prices rise 5%. What is the real return?
Your savings earn 4% and prices rise 2%. Are you better off?
What is the real return?

answers.explanation: 2% minus 5% is -3%.
Your money grows faster than prices.
It shows what your money really buys.

cards.title: Do not put all your eggs in one basket
cards.text: Spreading money across many companies lowers the harm if one fails.

cards.title: Falls and recoveries
cards.text: Shares can fall a lot in one year and recover over several.

cards.title: Stay the course
cards.text: People who sell after a crash often miss the recovery.

facts.text: You can split your £20,000 yearly ISA allowance between cash and investments.
facts.source_label: gov.uk · Individual Savings Accounts

quiz.text: The market falls 30%. What did long-term investors usually do best by?
Which is less risky?
Why spread your money?

choices.text: To lower the harm if one investment fails

answers.explanation: Markets have usually recovered over several years.
One company can fail. Many rarely fail together.
Spreading risk protects you from one bad pick.

cards.title: A little each month
cards.text: Investing a fixed amount each month buys more shares when prices are low.

cards.title: No guessing
cards.text: It takes the guesswork out of choosing a good time to invest.

facts.text: You can pay up to £4,000 a year into a Lifetime ISA, for example a bit each month.
facts.source_label: gov.uk · Lifetime ISA

quiz.text: Prices fall and you invest the same £100. Do you buy more or fewer shares?
What does drip feeding avoid?

choices.text: Guessing the best time to invest

quiz.text: What is drip feeding?

choices.text: Investing a fixed amount on a regular date

answers.explanation: Each share costs less, so £100 buys more.
It removes timing, not all risk.
You invest a set amount on a schedule.

cards.title: Lending for a return
cards.text: A bond is a loan to a government or a company. It pays a fixed interest rate until it ends.

cards.title: Rates move prices
cards.text: When interest rates rise, existing bonds fall in price.

facts.text: The Bank of England's Bank Rate is 3.75%. When it rises, new bonds pay more and old bonds fall in price.
facts.source_label: Bank of England · Interest rates and Bank Rate

facts.text: Bonds can be held in a stocks and shares ISA, inside the £20,000 yearly ISA allowance.
facts.source_label: gov.uk · Individual Savings Accounts

quiz.text: Interest rates rise sharply. What happens to the price of old bonds?
What is a government bond?
What does a bond usually pay?

answers.explanation: New bonds pay more, so old ones are worth less.
You lend money and get interest back.
Most bonds pay a set rate until they end.

cards.title: Money for later
cards.text: A pension is savings you can use when you are older.

cards.title: Free money from work
cards.text: Your employer adds to your workplace pension when you pay in.

cards.title: Start early
cards.text: Money paid in early has the longest time to grow.

facts.text: With auto-enrolment, at least 8% of your qualifying pay goes into your workplace pension.
facts.source_label: gov.uk · Workplace pensions: what you and your employer pay

facts.text: Your employer must pay at least 3% of that.
facts.source_label: gov.uk · Workplace pensions: what you and your employer pay

facts.text: Pension payments get tax relief, so at the basic rate of 20%, £80 from you becomes £100 in your pension.
facts.source_label: gov.uk · Income Tax rates and allowances

quiz.text: Who adds money to a workplace pension?
You pay £80 into a pension at the basic rate. How much goes in?
Why start a pension early?

answers.explanation: Your employer pays in too.
Tax relief adds 20% of the total, so £80 becomes £100.
Early money has the most years to grow.

cards.title: You are your biggest asset
cards.text: Skills you learn can raise your pay for the rest of your working life.

cards.title: Costs now, pays later
cards.text: A course costs money now and may pay back over many years.

facts.text: With a Plan 5 student loan, you repay only on what you earn above £25,000 a year.
facts.source_label: gov.uk · Rates and thresholds for employers 2026 to 2027

quiz.text: A £1,000 course raises your pay £1,000 a year. When has it paid back?
What is your biggest money asset when you are young?
Is a course always worth it?

choices.text: Check what it costs and how much it may raise pay

answers.explanation: One year of higher pay covers the cost.
Your future pay is worth far more than what you own now.
Compare the cost with the likely pay rise.

cards.title: Exchange rates move
cards.text: The pound buys more or less abroad as exchange rates change.

cards.title: Weak pound, dearer trips
cards.text: A weaker pound makes holidays and imported goods cost more.

cards.title: Fees add up
cards.text: Card fees for spending abroad add to the cost. Check before you travel.

facts.text: About 23.9% of students at UK universities come from outside the UK (HESA 2024/25), so exchange rates matter to many.
facts.source_label: HESA · Where students come from

quiz.text: The pound falls against the dollar. A US holiday costs...
Your family sends money from abroad and their currency falls. What happens?
What adds to the cost of spending abroad?

answers.explanation: Each pound buys fewer dollars.
Their money converts to fewer pounds.

cards.title: Gross and net
